summary: The incident was caused by an expired client TLS certificate used by payment-service to authenticate to the bank-partner-api, leading to mTLS handshake failures and payment failures despite a normal HTTP error-rate dashboard. Evidence from multiple verified observations (F1, F2, F3, F4, F10) supports this conclusion with a confidence of 0.60. Immediate certificate renewal and longer‑term automation are recommended.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Expired client certificate for bank-partner-api causing mTLS handshake failures
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The client TLS certificate used by payment-service to authenticate to bank-partner-api expired at 12:15, causing mTLS handshake rejections. Payment-service treats these as business failures, marking payments PENDING_RETRY and returning errors that do not increment the HTTP error-rate metric, while the internal bank_api_error_rate metric spikes to 100%. Customers experience payment failures despite a green error-rate dashboard.

causal_chain.claim: mTLS handshake with bank-partner-api rejected due to expired cert
Payment-service marks payments PENDING_RETRY and returns business‑logic errors (not 5xx)
bank_api_error_rate metric spikes to 100% from 12:16 onward
Overall HTTP error_rate remains low, so dashboard appears normal
Customers see payment failures and open tickets

assumptions: Payment-service uses the expired client certificate for all calls to bank-partner-api
Business‑logic errors (e.g., PENDING_RETRY) are not counted in the HTTP error_rate metric

ranked_hypotheses.title: Bank‑partner‑API outage or latency spike (dependency failure)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The external bank-partner-api experienced an outage or severe latency spike, causing payment-service calls to fail or timeout. These failures are recorded in the bank_api_error_rate metric, leading to customer‑visible payment failures while the HTTP error‑rate metric stays low.

causal_chain.claim: Bank‑partner‑API became unavailable or highly latent
Payment failures are reported by customers

assumptions: The mTLS handshake failure observed in F1 is a symptom of the bank API being down rather than a certificate issue

facts.statement: The first payment processing error occurred at 2026-04-02T12:15:27Z, marking the payment PENDING_RETRY due to a rejected mTLS handshake with bank-partner-api.
TLS expiration errors were logged at 2026-04-02T12:16:44Z, indicating the client certificate expired at 2026-04-02T12:15:00Z.
The `bank_api_error_rate` metric spiked to 100% starting at the 12:16 bucket and remained at 100%, while the overall HTTP `error_rate` stayed below 0.32%.
`latency_p99_ms` for payment-service did not spike; it actually decreased after the failures began.
`request_rate` for payment-service remained roughly constant (~100 req/s) throughout the incident window.

timeline.event: Configuration change: bank.api.timeout_ms increased from 3000 ms to 5000 ms.
Client TLS certificate used by payment-service expires.
First payment marked PENDING_RETRY due to mTLS handshake rejection.
TLS expiration error logged, confirming certificate expiry.
Support reports ~40 tickets of payment failures; incident declared SEV‑2.

recommended_actions.action: Generate and deploy a new client TLS certificate for payment-service to authenticate to bank-partner-api; restart payment-service to load the new certificate.
recommended_actions.rationale: The expired certificate is the root cause of mTLS handshake failures (F1, F2). Renewing it will restore successful downstream calls.

recommended_actions.action: Verify that payment-service correctly propagates downstream failures to the HTTP `error_rate` metric or adjust monitoring to surface `bank_api_error_rate` on the primary dashboard.
recommended_actions.rationale: Customers see failures while the main dashboard stays green; aligning metrics will improve observability (F3, F4).

recommended_actions.action: Implement automated certificate rotation and expiry alerts (e.g., Prometheus alert on cert expiry < 24h).
recommended_actions.rationale: Prevents recurrence of expiry‑related outages (root cause).

recommended_actions.action: Add a dedicated `bank_api_latency_p99_ms` metric and integrate it into dashboards.
recommended_actions.rationale: Current latency metrics (F11) do not isolate downstream latency; this will aid future root‑cause analysis.

data_gaps: Configuration changes for bank-partner-api and kafka were not queried; unknown if any recent changes could have contributed.
No dedicated latency metric for bank-partner-api calls, limiting ability to confirm downstream latency spikes.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Evidence that the client certificate was still valid at the time of failures (e.g., a valid cert fingerprint log).
Logs from bank-partner-api showing it was down or rejecting connections for reasons unrelated to client cert expiry.

findings.statement: The bank_api_error_rate metric spikes to 100% starting at the 12:16 bucket and stays at 100% through the rest of the window, whereas the overall HTTP error_rate stays below 0.32%.
The error_rate dashboard for payment-service shows no abnormal rise (max 0.32%) despite the high bank_api_error_rate, explaining why the panel appears green while customers experience failures.
payment-service depends downstream on ledger-db (shared DB), bank-partner-api (external), and kafka (queue produce).
No deployments of payment-service or its downstream services (ledger-db, bank-partner-api, kafka) occurred in the past 24 hours; only settlement-service was deployed at 2026-04-02T10:30:00Z.
payment-service configuration changed: bank.api.timeout_ms increased from 3000 ms to 5000 ms at 2026-04-02T11:20:00Z.
No configuration changes were recorded for ledger-db in the past 24 hours.
No deployments were recorded for bank-partner-api in the past 24 hours.
The payment-service metric `bank_api_error_rate` jumps from ~0.2% to 25.15% (max 100%) in the 12:12 bucket and reaches 100% steady from the 12:16 bucket onward.
The `latency_p99_ms` metric for payment-service does not show a spike at the onset; it drops from ~300 ms before 12:12 to ~140 ms after 12:16 and remains roughly stable.
`request_rate` for payment-service stays roughly constant (~100 req/s) throughout the window, indicating traffic volume did not drop when failures began.
